notice: The selected findings below were checked against retrieved official reports, publisher full text or indexed primary-publication abstracts. They inform design; they are not Eumo outcome data.
feedbackNotice: Qualitative project-owner feedback; participant count and study protocol were not supplied.

themes.label: Community & accountability
themes.headline: Progress is easier to act on when it is visible.
themes.summary: Progress-monitoring interventions improved goal attainment; reported or public progress was associated with larger effects.
themes.design: Optional friend visibility and study records.
themes.limit: Goal monitoring is not the same intervention as live co-study or online friend status.

themes.label: AI learning support
themes.headline: Structured AI can support learning.
themes.summary: A tailored AI tutor produced more than twice the median learning gains of an active-learning class in a 194-student physics trial.
themes.design: Explore guided questions, task breakdown and feedback in optional AI chat.
themes.limit: The tested educational tutor is different from Eumo’s open-ended companion chat.

themes.label: AI companionship
themes.headline: Users describe company and support.
themes.summary: A thematic analysis of 1,854 reviews and 66 user responses identified companionship and emotional support.
themes.design: A persistent character with optional conversation.
themes.limit: Reported experiences, not an efficacy rate or a learning result.

themes.label: Rewards & motivation
themes.headline: Game elements can support motivation.
themes.summary: A learning-gamification meta-analysis found a positive motivational effect across 16 studies and 2,246 participants.
themes.design: Make effort visible through discoveries and personalization.
themes.limit: A standardized effect size, not a percentage; effects concern gamification packages, not rewards alone.

sources.citation: OECD (2023). PISA 2022 Results (Volume II): Learning During – and From – Disruption.
sources.status: Verified official executive summary and report
sources.finding: 30% of students, on average across OECD countries, reported distraction from using digital devices in most or every mathematics lesson.
sources.scope: Self-reported classroom distraction; not a causal effect or prevalence estimate for the entire 8–35 target range.

sources.citation: Harkin, B., et al. (2016). Does monitoring goal progress promote goal attainment? A meta-analysis of the experimental evidence. Psychological Bulletin, 142(2), 198–229.
sources.status: Verified indexed primary abstract and Crossref metadata
sources.finding: 138 randomized studies (N = 19,951); goal-attainment effect d = 0.40, 95% CI [0.32, 0.48]. Effects were larger when progress was reported or made public and physically recorded.
sources.population: Participants across goal-monitoring intervention studies; not a single age-defined student sample.
sources.scope: Progress monitoring across contexts, not an experiment on Eumo, Zoom study rooms or body doubling. Public reporting is a moderator, and d is not a percentage.

sources.citation: Kestin, G., Miller, K., Klales, A., Milbourne, T., & Ponti, G. (2025). AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting. Scientific Reports, 15, 17458.
sources.finding: The purpose-built AI tutor produced more than twice the median learning gains of in-class active learning.
sources.population: 194 Harvard undergraduate physics students; counterbalanced randomized comparison across two lessons.
sources.scope: Structured pedagogical tutoring, not generic companion chat. Does not establish Eumo effects, long-term benefits or equivalent results for all ages/subjects. The study does not justify saying half the time.

sources.citation: Ta, V., et al. (2020). User Experiences of Social Support From Companion Chatbots in Everyday Contexts: Thematic Analysis. Journal of Medical Internet Research, 22(3), e16235.
sources.finding: Users described companionship and emotional, informational and appraisal support.
sources.population: Study 1: 1,854 Replika reviews. Study 2: open-ended responses from 66 Replika users.
sources.scope: Separate qualitative datasets from self-selected users, not 1,920 interviewed participants, population prevalence, causal efficacy or measured learning gains.

sources.citation: Sailer, M., & Homner, L. (2020). The Gamification of Learning: a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 77–112.
sources.finding: Motivational outcomes: Hedges’ g = 0.36, 95% CI [0.18, 0.54]; 16 studies, N = 2,246.
sources.population: Participants in the learning-gamification studies included in the motivational outcome analysis.
sources.scope: Gamification combines multiple game elements; it does not isolate rewards or compare all rewards with punishment. g is not a percentage. Motivational effects were less stable in a more rigorous subset.

sources.citation: Steel, P. (2007). The nature of procrastination: a meta-analytic and theoretical review of quintessential self-regulatory failure. Psychological Bulletin, 133(1), 65–94.
sources.status: Verified indexed primary abstract and Crossref metadata
sources.finding: A review of 691 correlations identified task aversiveness, task delay, self-efficacy, impulsiveness and related self-regulation factors among consistent predictors.
sources.population: Studies included in the procrastination review; no single age cohort.
sources.scope: Supports a broader problem framing; no student prevalence statistic is used.

competitors.name: Pomodoro technique
competitors.lens: Timed focus, breaks, planning and reflection
competitors.scope: The technique itself is not punitive; separate product-specific penalties from the method.

competitors.name: Forest
competitors.lens: An example of a penalty in a focus app
competitors.finding: During strict sessions, leaving the app or using blocked apps may make the tree wither.
competitors.scope: Forest also has group focus; do not generalize the absence of peer features to all focus apps.

competitors.name: Cat On Chair: Pomodoro Timer
competitors.lens: Cat companionship, timers, gifts and room decoration
competitors.status: Publisher description in official Apple software API verified 2026-11-17
competitors.finding: Both Pomodoro and count-up modes, gifts/rewards and furniture. Failed sessions may produce trash.
competitors.scope: No live human peer-presence feature is listed; this is not an exhaustive feature audit.

market.target: Learners aged 8–35 who want support for independent study and work.
market.status: Requested product target, not a measured market estimate; studies do not validate effects for this entire age range.
market.persona: Alex, 20: illustrative profile informed by project feedback, not an interviewed participant.
market.business: Planned free core with optional subscription, digital collections and physical-product revenue.

productStatus.cloud: Four-digit Canele pairing and device-to-web progress import are deployed; pairing requires confirmation on the device.
productStatus.hardware: Updated firmware and real-device pairing/sync verification remain to be completed on the connected computer.
productStatus.boundary: This is not general account-based save synchronization between independent browsers.
productStatus.rewards: Active Study / Work timer time earns progress. Paused time and Break do not. Ending early preserves already-earned rewards.

Test pricing and repeat use before claiming commercial demand.
